requirements.statement: For each prerecorded synchronized media whose synchronized captions are delivered through a <track> element, outside the particular cases of the criterion, that <track> element has kind="captions".

citations.quote: Pour chaque média temporel synchronisé pré-enregistré possédant des sous-titres synchronisés diffusés via une balise `<track>`, la balise `<track>` possède-t-elle un attribut `kind="captions"`
(hors cas particuliers)

routes.statement: The <track> element that delivers the captions has a kind attribute with the value captions.

citations.quote: la balise `<track>` possède-t-elle un attribut `kind="captions"`
le sous-titrage pour sourds et malentendants (attribut kind="captions" de la balise <track> en HTML5, par exemple)

rationale.text: The test applies to media whose synchronized captions are delivered through a <track> element, and asks whether that element has kind="captions". The glossary on captions draws the line: kind="subtitles" is for translation, kind="captions" for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and only the latter counts. The methodology writes kind="caption" in the singular, which HTML does not define; the entry follows the wording. No fault is mechanical. A track with another kind fails the test only if it carries captions for deaf and hard-of-hearing users; if it carries translation subtitles, chapters or metadata, the media has no captions through a <track> element and the test does not apply to it. Telling the two apart needs someone to read the track, and a custom player may render captions from a metadata track. The custom check custom/4-3-track-kind-captions therefore never faults. It reads the kind of every <track> child of a media element on the page, nested documents and shadow trees included. When the page has no such track, no media has captions delivered through one, and the check answers inapplicable. When it has one, the check answers cannot_tell, whatever the kind. It never answers no_fault, and that is a correction. An earlier version answered no_fault when every track was labelled captions. Its link names the route and every particular case with whole scope, so it is a resolving link, and its no_fault would have counted as proof that the requirement holds. But a no_fault must rest on at least one element the requirement applies to, and this check cannot show that any track is one: it does not load the track, and it cannot tell whether the media is prerecorded, synchronized rather than video-only, carries information, or falls under a particular case. A page whose only media is a decorative, live or video-only video with a kind="captions" track would have been answered no_fault, and the tool would have said passed where the test does not apply. Two fixes were possible: correct the check's outcome, or make the link partial. The outcome is what was false, so the check record was corrected. Partial scope would be untrue: the check looks at every <track> child of a media element, which are all the elements the requirement can apply to, since captions delivered through a <track> element need such a track. The link keeps the route and the particular cases with whole scope: the check accounts for every such element, and abstains on all of them. It is evidence only because it never faults. The entry stays at none. A check that never answers no_fault cannot meet the rule that every accepted route of a full entry can pass, and no fault is mechanical. What would raise it: a way to establish, with the media prerequisite, that a media with a captions track is a prerecorded synchronized media that carries information and that its track holds captions, so that the check can name an element in scope before it answers no_fault. Applicability is judgment: the absence of any <track> element does make the test not applicable with certainty, but the presence of one does not make it applicable. Needs is empty: the check reads attributes on the page as loaded.
